# Station plots and readouts

Station plot (i) notes. "The variable" and "the station" stand for the page's selected variable and station. Times are stored in UTC and labeled in New York time. All data are provisional and may be revised.

## Water quality at the buoys

(method-yoy)=
### This year against earlier years

Shows
: The variable at the selected depth, this year against every earlier year on the same calendar dates, from 96 days back to 14 days ahead. This year is the bold line; earlier years run from the most recent to the oldest.

Method
: Each line is a trailing 36-hour mean of hourly means, with at least 24 of the 36 hours present; gaps stay gaps. A year is drawn only when at least 80% of the window has data. Full record draws every year end to end.

Sources
: The station, LISICOS, University of Connecticut {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`, with our own saved downloads where the server no longer publishes the early record.

Caveats
: Years with less than 80% coverage are listed under the plot, not drawn.

For salinity
: Salinity is on the practical salinity scale, which has no unit.

For dissolved oxygen
: Dissolved oxygen in mg/L.

References: [1] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`.

(method-chg)=
### 7-day change

Shows
: The change in the 36-hour mean of the variable at the selected depth over the past week, this year against earlier years, over the last 60 days. Zero is no change.

Method
: The 36-hour mean now minus the same mean 168 hours earlier; year and coverage rules as for the year comparison.

Sources
: The station, LISICOS {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`.

For salinity
: Salinity is on the practical salinity scale, which has no unit.

For dissolved oxygen
: Dissolved oxygen in mg/L.

References: [1] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`.

(method-col)=
### Water column

Shows
: The variable at each depth the station measures, recent weeks. Faint lines are hourly means; bold lines are 36-hour means.

Method
: Hourly means of the readings that pass quality control; 36-hour means as for the year comparison. Quality control: Gross-range checks (temperature -2 to 35 °C, salinity 5 to 36, dissolved oxygen 0 to 20 mg/L), narrowed where the waterway sets its own range. A spike test drops a reading more than 1.5 °C, 1.5 salinity or 2 mg/L from the median of the 13 readings around it (about 3 hours). A placeholder test drops a run of whole-number readings; real sensor values carry decimals, and the server has published day counts in a salinity column. Flat-line tests are not applied.

Sources
: The station, LISICOS {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`.

For salinity
: Salinity is on the practical salinity scale, which has no unit.

For dissolved oxygen
: Dissolved oxygen in mg/L. Shading marks reference levels: under 1 mg/L anoxic and under 3 mg/L hypoxic, as the Long Island Sound Partnership defines them {ref}`[2] <ref-lisp2024hypoxia>`; under 4.8 mg/L, EPA's criterion for continuous exposure that protects growth from Cape Cod to Cape Hatteras. These are levels for reading the plot, not a regulatory assessment. Summer hypoxia and its history in the western Sound: {ref}`[3] <ref-epa_roe_hypoxia>` {ref}`[4] <ref-wilson2008hypoxia>` {ref}`[5] <ref-anderson2001pulses>`.

References: [1] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`; [2] {ref}`Long Island Sound Partnership, hypoxia indicator <ref-lisp2024hypoxia>`; [3] {ref}`U.S. EPA (2023), Report on the Environment: hypoxia <ref-epa_roe_hypoxia>`; [4] {ref}`Wilson, Swanson and Crowley (2008), long-term variation of western-Sound hypoxia <ref-wilson2008hypoxia>`; [5] {ref}`Anderson and Taylor (2001), nutrient pulses, blooms and seasonal hypoxia <ref-anderson2001pulses>`.

(method-sb)=
### Surface minus bottom

Shows
: Surface the variable minus bottom the variable, hourly and as a 36-hour mean.

Method
: For temperature, a working definition of stratification over the last 24 hours: mixed under 0.3 °C, weakly stratified to 1.0 °C, stratified above. Salinity and oxygen are drawn without thresholds.

Sources
: The station, LISICOS {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`.

Caveats
: The thresholds are a working definition, not a published standard. The Sound's stratification and mixing: {ref}`[2] <ref-odonnell2013physical>` {ref}`[3] <ref-torgersen1997mixing>`.

References: [1] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`; [2] {ref}`O'Donnell et al. (2013), The Physical Oceanography of Long Island Sound <ref-odonnell2013physical>`; [3] {ref}`Torgersen, DeAngelo and O'Donnell (1997), mixing and the controls on western-Sound hypoxia <ref-torgersen1997mixing>`.

(method-bturb)=
### Turbidity at the buoys

Shows
: Hourly median turbidity at about 1 m at each buoy, in NTU; faint where the day is flagged as likely sensor fouling.

Method
: Readings that repeat one value for 2 hours or more are dropped as stuck. A day whose quietest tenth of readings sits above 5 NTU is flagged as likely fouling. The axis stops at a cap; higher readings run along the top edge, with the value on hover.

Sensors
: The turbidity channel of the Sea-Bird ECO FLNTU (chlorophyll fluorescence and turbidity) at the surface of each buoy {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`.

Caveats
: In warm water the optical window fouls within weeks and the reading climbs though the water has not changed; servicing drops it back in one step. The fouling flag is a provisional rule and has not been reconciled with LISICOS servicing records. Turbidity in the Sound's bays and harbors is measured by Save the Sound's Unified Water Study {ref}`[2] <ref-sts_monitoring>`.

References: [1] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`; [2] {ref}`Save the Sound, water quality monitoring programs <ref-sts_monitoring>`.

## Weather and waves

(method-next48)=
### Wind

Shows
: Wind and gusts at the station: measured over the last day and a half, and forecast by NOAA's HRRR model for the next two days. The stitched forecast (the bold blue line) takes each hour from the newest run that reaches it; the lavender lines either side show how far such a forecast typically misses at that lead time; dots are gusts (gray measured, lavender HRRR's, green GFS's). Each faint line is an earlier HRRR run: where they bunch together, the model has been consistent; where they spread apart, it has not, and the timing or strength is less certain. The slider at the top left picks a run (so does hovering its line) and draws it dashed, with the time it was issued; the expanded chart pans back through a week of runs. Revisions, a switch on the plot, opens a small chart of how the forecast for one hour, the one under the pointer or the page's time, changed from run to run: along its bottom is the time each run was issued, so a line rising to the right is the model raising that hour's wind as it drew nearer; once the hour has passed, a gold dot is the wind measured then; past HRRR's reach the chart is GFS's, its runs of the last 30 hours, 6 hours apart. Past the last hour HRRR reaches, NOAA's GFS model carries the forecast on in green, with its own typical miss shaded in a paler green; "7 days", a switch on the plot, widens it to a week ahead. From now to HRRR's last hour the green line runs beside it, GFS for the same hours, so where the two models meet, a step between them reads as their difference in timing or strength; both models' gusts are drawn over HRRR's last day. Before now a thinner green line is GFS's last forecast before each hour, and with Revisions on GFS's earlier runs are drawn faint across the whole window, as HRRR's are. Along the bottom, a thin, faint brick strip marks the hours the forecast reaches the National Weather Service's level for a small craft advisory (25 kt) or a gale warning (34 kt, darker), and a stronger strip the hours an advisory is in force for the station's marine zone (darker for a gale).

Method
: HRRR (3 km, run every hour) is read at the station's nearest water cells {ref}`[1] <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`. Hourly runs reach 18 hours ahead and the 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC runs 48, so beyond 18 hours the stitched forecast comes from the latest 48-hour run, which can be up to 6 hours older than the newest. The plot keeps every run of the last day and the 48-hour runs of the last week. The typical error is the mean absolute difference between HRRR and the four buoys at each lead time since January 2024; about 6 in 10 forecast hours fall within it. GFS {ref}`[2] <ref-noaa2026gfs>` (0.25 degree, about 28 by 20 km here, run every 6 hours) is read the same way, from NOAA's open data {ref}`[3] <ref-noaa2026gfsaws>`, at its four nearest water cells, every 3 hours to 168 hours ahead, and linearly between; its typical miss is measured at the four buoys at its own lead times (6 to 168 hours) since January 2024: about 3.4 kt at 6 hours, rising to 5.0 kt at 168 (the Forecast verification page sets it beside HRRR's).

Caveats
: Uncorrected model output: HRRR to 48 hours, then GFS, never blended. Not a substitute for the National Weather Service marine forecast. HRRR is used first for its 3 km grid, run hourly; GFS's cells are one or two across a Sound 5 to 34 km wide, so it smooths the wind over the water, and at the buoys it reads slightly low (a bias of about −0.5 to −1.1 kt by lead time, uncorrected on the plot). Where the two models meet, the step between them is the models' difference, not a change in the weather. The advisory levels are NWS's criteria for sustained wind; NWS issues advisories from its own forecast, also for seas, so the forecast reaching a level is not an advisory, and an advisory can be in force below it.

References: [1] {ref}`Dowell et al. (2022), the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`; [2] {ref}`NOAA EMC, the Global Forecast System (GFS) <ref-noaa2026gfs>`; [3] {ref}`NOAA, GFS on the Registry of Open Data on AWS <ref-noaa2026gfsaws>`.

(method-wind)=
### Wind record

Shows
: Wind speed at the station: a smoothed line, the hourly wind (faint) and each day's strongest gust (dots). Hovering gives the direction it blows from.

Method
: The bold line is hourly for the last two days, then smoothed more the older it is: a two-sided exponential moving average whose half-life widens from 1 hour two days back to 6 hours two weeks back and a day a month back, so recent hours keep their detail and earlier weeks read as a trend. The average runs forward and back so peaks are not delayed, and restarts after a gap. Where the station has no reading, a dashed line gives HRRR's last forecast before each hour (the run issued 1 hour before) at the station {ref}`[1] <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`, from January 2024: the model's stand-in for the record, never a measurement. Against the four buoys over the 100 days to October 2026 it was within 2.4 to 2.8 kt on average (mean absolute error) with a bias under 1 kt.

Caveats
: The plot shows the last 100 days. Speeds follow the Units switch. Directions are turned to true north: the server's read about 14 degrees clockwise of NDBC's records of the same buoys, close to the local magnetic variation. Shading marks the NWS marine advisories in force for the station's zone (see the Advisory readout's note).

References: [1] {ref}`Dowell et al. (2022), the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`.

(method-air)=
### Air and water temperature

Shows
: Hourly air temperature and surface water temperature. Where the station has no air reading, a dashed line gives HRRR's 2 m air temperature from its last forecast before each hour (a model, not a measurement) {ref}`[1] <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`.

Sources
: The station's weather sensors and its surface sensor; NOAA HRRR for the dashed stand-in.

References: [1] {ref}`Dowell et al. (2022), the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`.

(method-pressure)=
### Pressure tendency

Shows
: How fast the barometer is changing: the change over 3 hours, observed and then forecast by HRRR (dashed). A falling barometer comes before wind; the faster it falls, the more.

Method
: Observed: the station's hourly mean minus that of 3 hours before. Forecast: the same from HRRR's sea-level pressure at the station. Shaded bands follow the UK shipping forecast's terms: steady to falling slowly under 1.6 mb in 3 hours, quickly 3.6 to 6, very rapidly beyond 6.

Caveats
: The buoy barometer and HRRR's sea-level pressure differ by up to about 1 mb, so the dashed line can start a little off the observed one. Where the station has no reading, a fainter dashed line gives the same change from HRRR's last forecast before each hour (a model stand-in, not a measurement).

(method-waves)=
### Waves

Shows
: Significant wave height each hour, and each hour's highest single wave (faint). Hovering gives the dominant period.

Method
: Significant height is the mean of the highest third of the waves, close to what an observer reports. Ahead of the last reading, and while the sensor is out, the NWS model line is the Nearshore Wave Prediction System (SWAN) at the buoy's nearest water cell, each hour from the newest run that covers it (runs at 00 and 12 UTC) {ref}`[1] <ref-booij1999swan>`. The NECOFS line is NECOFS's wave forecast at the mesh node nearest the buoy, from its newest daily run (about 4.5 days ahead when posted); hovering gives its mean period, which runs shorter than a peak period by definition.

Caveats
: The wave datasets have been unpublished on the data server for long stretches; the record before an outage comes from our saved downloads, and the page checks every hour. Heights follow the Units switch. Wave growth in the western Sound is fetch-limited and larger under easterly winds {ref}`[2] <ref-shin2021waves>`. The model lines are models, not measurements; neither is yet scored against the buoys.

References: [1] {ref}`Booij, Ris and Holthuijsen (1999), the SWAN wave model <ref-booij1999swan>`; [2] {ref}`Shin et al. (2021), Waves in Western Long Island Sound: A Fetch-Limited Coastal Basin <ref-shin2021waves>`.

(method-model)=
### Model values while a buoy is out

Shows
: While a buoy's sensor is out, the table, readouts and map show what a model gives at the buoy for the same hour, under the fault and marked as a model. They are not measurements, and the outage stays shown as one.

Method
: Wind, gusts, air temperature and pressure: the newest NOAA HRRR run (3 km) that covers the hour, read at the buoy; now that is a run issued about an hour before. Waves: the newest run of the NWS Nearshore Wave Prediction System (SWAN on a 1.8 km grid, run by NWS New York at 00 and 12 UTC) at the water cell nearest the buoy, at most 0.4 km away.

Sources
: NOAA HRRR; NWS Nearshore Wave Prediction System (NOAA NOMADS). Every NWPS run is archived as published.

Caveats
: HRRR's typical error at each lead is measured against the buoys' own records (the Forecast verification page). NWPS is forced by the forecasters' wind grids rather than by observations and has not been verified against the buoys' wave records, which are unavailable while their wave sensors are out.

(method-advisory)=
### NWS marine advisories

Shows
: The advisory or warning NWS New York has in force for the station's forecast zone, and (shaded behind the wind plot) the ones in force over the plotted days: small craft advisories lighter, gale and stronger warnings darker.

Method
: Each event is merged from the products that issued, extended or canceled it, from its earliest start to its latest end. Each station takes the marine zone that contains it, or the nearest (harbor gauges lie inside the coastline). Before April 2021 the eastern Sound was one zone (ANZ330), and its events stand for both of today's.

Sources
: NWS New York (OKX) VTEC products, from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive (2005 on); zone outlines from api.weather.gov.

Caveats
: An advisory is a forecast decision for a whole zone, not a measurement at the station. Two archive rows (one 2012 event whose end the archive lost) are left out.

(method-trends)=
### Trends and %iles

Shows
: Under each reading, which way it is heading and how unusual it is for the time of year. The arrow's angle gives the rate: flat for no change, a gentle slope for a slow change, 45 degrees for a steady one, steep for a sudden one; up for rising, down for falling, with the signed change beside it. For wind, ↻ is veering (the wind shifting clockwise) and ↺ backing (counterclockwise), with the degrees. The %ile ranks the value against the same dates in earlier years.

Method
: Direction compares two adjacent windows sized to how fast each quantity moves: 3 hours for wind, waves and pressure (the last 3 hours' mean against the 3 before for wind and waves); 24 hours for air and water. Thresholds (no change, then slow, steady and sudden): wind 2, 5 and 10 kt; waves 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6 m; pressure 1, 2 and 3 mb; air 2, 6 and 12°F; water temperature 0.2, 0.8 and 2°F; salinity 0.05, 0.2 and 0.6; oxygen 0.2, 0.8 and 2 mg/L. A wind shift is shown when the mean direction of the last 3 hours differs from the 3 before by 20 degrees or more, in wind of 5 kt or more. The %ile ranks the value (the 36-hour mean for water; the last 3 days' mean for wind and waves; the last day's for air and pressure) against the same dates, a week either side, in every earlier year with data for at least half that fortnight. Weather %iles use daily means: from the NDBC archives of the same buoys (Western and Central Sound from 2004, Execution Rocks from 2005), then the buoys' own records.

Caveats
: A %ile needs at least three earlier years; where a station has fewer it reads "-- %ile" (the Stamford buoy's weather starts in 2024).

## Tides and currents

(method-hilo)=
### Highs and lows

Shows
: Each high and low tide: NOAA's prediction (faint) and the water's (bold), against mean higher high water and the NWS minor flood level.

Method
: The observed high or low is the highest or lowest hourly mean within 2 hours of the predicted time.

Sources
: NOAA CO-OPS; flood levels from the National Weather Service.

Caveats
: Observations are preliminary until NOAA verifies them.

(method-dep)=
### Departure from prediction

Shows
: Observed water level minus NOAA's prediction, hourly: what wind, pressure and river flow add to the tide.

Method
: The prediction is averaged over the same hour as the observed hourly mean.

Sources
: NOAA CO-OPS.

Caveats
: Predictions use the 1983 to 2001 tidal epoch; sea level has risen about 0.3 ft since, so the departure sits above zero most weeks.

(method-mflow)=
### Current against prediction and model

Shows
: At NOAA's current meter at Groton, in the Thames River: the measured current (gold) at the bin 38 m out from the pier, NOAA's tidal current prediction for that bin (blue) and the NECOFS model's surface current at the nearest model element (teal, dashed), all along the meter's flood direction (310 degrees, up the river): above the line is flood, below it ebb. The arrows above the plot give the measured direction each hour (faint under 0.05 knots, where it wanders). The note in the expanded plot and the readouts score the prediction and the model against the meter.

Method
: Measured: the meter's 6-minute readings resolved along and across the flood direction and each part averaged by the hour; the two give the hour's speed and direction. The comparison uses the hours where both have a value: the root-mean-square difference; flood and ebb strength as the 90th percentile of the current's size each way, the estimate's over the meter's; and slack timing as the mean time from each of the meter's slacks to the estimate's nearest slack of the same turn (within 3 hours, interpolated between hours). The plot's note scores the hours on screen; the readouts score the last 14 days.

Sources
: NOAA CO-OPS: New London PORTS current meter nl0101 and NOAA's tidal current predictions for it. NECOFS/UMASSD: FVCOM, UMass Dartmouth {ref}`[1] <ref-chen2006fvcom>`.

Caveats
: A river mouth: the current is weak (about half a knot at most) and the river's flow adds to the ebb, and NOAA notes that its predictions err more where currents are weak and during high runoff. The meter reads 5.2 m below the surface; the model's value is its surface layer. Hourly means smooth the timing of slack. Readings faster than 4 m/s are left out as bad pings; gaps stay gaps.

References: [1] {ref}`Chen, Beardsley and Cowles (2006), the FVCOM system <ref-chen2006fvcom>`.

(method-mfan)=
### Seen from above

Shows
: The Groton current meter from above, north up, at the page's time, on NOAA's chart: land, piers, depth contours (meters below mean lower low water) and the dredged channel, faintly; the meter's beam out into the channel to scale; and at each of its ten bins an arrow for the hour's current (gold), its length on the speed scale. The heavier arrow is the bin NOAA predicts; NOAA's prediction for it is the dashed blue arrow, along NOAA's flood or ebb direction. A hollow dot is a bin with no reading that hour. Move the time bar to watch the current turn across the channel.

Method
: Each bin's 6-minute readings resolved along and across the flood direction (310 degrees) and averaged by the hour; speed and direction from the two parts.

Sources
: NOAA CO-OPS: New London PORTS current meter nl0101 and NOAA's tidal current predictions for it. The chart: NOAA Electronic Navigational Chart US5CT1FV (1:12,000), public domain; not for navigation.

Caveats
: NOAA does not publish which way the meter's beams point. The charted pier has two faces within 4 m of the meter's position; flow in the nearest bin runs along its south-west end (as flow beside a face must), so the drawing takes the beams as square to that end, out along the pier's axis into the channel (about 219 degrees). The arrows' directions are measured; only the bins' placement on the drawing rests on that bearing.

(method-mbins)=
### Across the channel

Shows
: Every bin of the Groton current meter, one line each: the current along the flood direction from 6 m out from the pier (strongest color) to 42 m (palest). The heavy line is the bin NOAA predicts. Where the lines part, the current runs faster toward mid-channel or turns earlier near the pier.

Method
: The meter is side-looking: mounted on the pier 5.2 m below the surface, it measures horizontally across the channel in 4 m bins. Each bin's 6-minute readings are resolved onto the flood direction (310 degrees) and averaged by the hour.

Sources
: NOAA CO-OPS: New London PORTS current meter nl0101.

Caveats
: NOAA predicts one bin only; the others are measurements alone.

## Rivers

(method-flow)=
### Flow against normal

Shows
: A river's flow against what is usual for each date: the median (middle line), 25th to 75th percentile (darker band) and 10th to 90th (lighter band).

Method
: Percentiles of daily mean flow for each calendar date, from the gauge's approved record.

Sources
: USGS Water Data for the Nation, the station.

Caveats
: Recent values are provisional until USGS approves them.

(method-share)=
### All rivers against normal

Shows
: Each river's flow as a percentile for its date, all rivers on one plot; 25 to 75 is normal.

Method
: Percentiles of daily mean flow for each calendar date, per river, from approved USGS record.

Sources
: USGS Water Data for the Nation.

(method-rpct)=
### Percentile for the date

Shows
: One river's flow as a percentile for its date, over time.

Method
: Percentiles of daily mean flow for each calendar date, from the gauge's approved record.

Sources
: USGS Water Data for the Nation, the station.

(method-ryoy)=
### This year against earlier years

Shows
: Daily mean flow this year against earlier years on the same dates.

Sources
: USGS Water Data for the Nation, the station.

(method-rturb)=
### River turbidity

Shows
: Hourly river turbidity in formazin nephelometric units (FNU), from a USGS sensor that is serviced and reviewed.

Sources
: USGS Water Data for the Nation.

Caveats
: FNU and the buoys' NTU are close but not identical units.

## A point on the map

(method-virtual-next48)=
### Wind

Shows
: HRRR wind and gusts (dots) at this point: before now, each hour's newest run; ahead, the stitched forecast. The band is HRRR's typical miss, borrowed from a scored buoy. "7 days" adds GFS (green) past HRRR's 48 hours.

Method
: HRRR's nearest water cell within 3 km {ref}`[1] <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`. The miss is the nearest scored buoy's within 25 km, else the four buoys' together, for GFS too. GFS {ref}`[2] <ref-noaa2026gfs>` at this point: the mean of its four nearest 0.25 degree water cells within 40 km, weighted by inverse distance squared, as at the stations.

Caveats
: Not scored at this point. Near the shore the real miss is larger.

References: [1] {ref}`Dowell et al. (2022), the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`; [2] {ref}`NOAA EMC, the Global Forecast System (GFS) <ref-noaa2026gfs>`.

(method-vwaves)=
### Waves, next 72 hours

Shows
: NWPS significant wave height at this point; arrows show where the waves travel.

Method
: The NWS wave model (SWAN) {ref}`[1] <ref-booij1999swan>`, nearest water cell within 2 km, newest run each hour.

Caveats
: Not scored on this site. Excludes currents, so wind against tide is not represented.

References: [1] {ref}`Booij, Ris and Holthuijsen (1999), the SWAN wave model <ref-booij1999swan>`.

(method-vcur)=
### Surface current, flood and ebb

Shows
: The surface current at this point along the flood direction, flood (into the Sound) up and ebb (out) down: measured by HF radar (gold dots, one per hour, joined faintly where hours are consecutive) against the NECOFS forecast, both as made a day ahead (dotted) and as the latest run (dashed). The shading between measured and forecast is the miss. The arrows along the top are the current's direction, where the water goes (gold measured, dashed teal forecast), not the wind's. Under the plot, the tide at the nearest shore gauge, observed and predicted, so flood and ebb can be read against high and low water and a wind's setup against the prediction.

Method
: HF radar: the 1 km cell holding the point, hourly totals from the NOAA IOOS HF Radar National Network (HFRNet; in the western Sound the University of Connecticut's LISICOS sites), served by NOAA NDBC. Hours where the cell is at the edge of that hour's coverage, or its geometry is weak (GDOP above 1.0), are drawn faint and left out of the comparison. NECOFS FVCOM (NECOFS/UMASSD) {ref}`[1] <ref-chen2003fvcom>` {ref}`[2] <ref-chen2006fvcom>`: the latest run on the triangle holding the point, every 2 hours; the forecast made a day ahead is, for each hour, the run fetched 24 to 48 hours before it, kept daily at the radar's cells. The flood direction is the radar's principal axis over its clean hours (the model's strongest current where the radar does not reach), with flood its westward end, toward the East River.

Sources
: HF radar: NOAA IOOS HFRNet totals from the University of Connecticut's LISICOS sites {ref}`[3] <ref-lisicos>`, served by NOAA NDBC. NECOFS/UMASSD: FVCOM, School for Marine Science and Technology, UMass Dartmouth {ref}`[1] <ref-chen2003fvcom>` {ref}`[2] <ref-chen2006fvcom>`.

Caveats
: The radar measures roughly the top meter, averaged over the hour and the cell; the model's top layer is a thin fraction of the local depth. Neither line is a reference for the tide's strength here, so the shading is a difference, not the forecast's error: against NOAA's current survey meters in the western Sound, the radar's tidal current has read from about two-thirds to 1.2 times as strong, by cell and season, and at some cells it runs at an angle to the Sound, while the model's has run 10 to 16% stronger. A change at the same cell from one week to the next, such as ebbs weakened by a northeast wind, is better evidence than a single gap. The comparison covers the radar's last 72 hours, so it is not a score. The radar reaches the western Sound only. The day-ahead forecast fills in once the site has kept runs for two days.

[The models behind the forecasts, their grids and how they score](https://longhorizon.blue/long-island-sound/forecasts/)

References: [1] {ref}`Chen, Liu and Beardsley (2003), FVCOM <ref-chen2003fvcom>`; [2] {ref}`Chen, Beardsley and Cowles (2006), the FVCOM system <ref-chen2006fvcom>`; [3] {ref}`LISICOS, University of Connecticut <ref-lisicos>`.

(method-vsst)=
### Water temperature, last 90 days

Shows
: Satellite sea surface temperature at this point, daily.

Method
: The MUR analysis {ref}`[1] <ref-chin2017mur>` {ref}`[2] <ref-jpl2015mur>`, the 1 km pixel holding the point.

Caveats
: The skin of the water, not 1 m down as at the buoys. Posted 1 to 3 days late.

References: [1] {ref}`Chin, Vazquez-Cuervo and Armstrong (2017), the MUR analysis <ref-chin2017mur>`; [2] {ref}`NASA/JPL (2015), MUR SST v4.1 <ref-jpl2015mur>`.

## Buoy sensors

Every sensor LISICOS lists for each buoy in its 2019 configuration {ref}`[1] <ref-lisicos>`.

Western Sound (WLIS)
: MSI 2.8 m buoy, 60 ft of water. Topside: RM Young anemometers (Marine and Heavy Duty); Campbell Scientific GPS16x-HVS; LI-COR 190R PAR. Surface: Sea-Bird SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO); SBE ECO FLNTU; SBE SUNA V2 nitrate; SBE HydroCycle PO4; Teledyne RDI ADCP 300 kHz; Neptune non-directional wave module. Mid-depth: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO), 27 ft. Bottom: Two SBE 37 MicroCATs (CTD, DO), 48 ft; Sunburst SAMI pCO2.

Execution Rocks (EXRX)
: MSI G-3000 buoy, 62 ft of water. Topside: RM Young anemometer (Marine); Campbell Scientific GPS16x-HVS; LI-COR 190R PAR. Surface: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO); SBE ECO FLNTU; SBE SUNA V2 nitrate; Teledyne RDI ADCP 600 kHz. Mid-depth: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO), 25 ft. Bottom: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO), 50 ft; SBE HydroCAT-EP.

ARTG buoy (ARTG)
: 91 ft of water. Topside: RM Young anemometer (Marine); Campbell Scientific GPS16x-HVS; LI-COR 190R PAR. Surface: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO); SBE ECO FLNTU; SBE SUNA V2 nitrate. Bottom: Two SBE 37 MicroCATs (CTD, DO), 78 ft.

Central Sound (CLIS)
: MSI G-5000 buoy, 90 ft of water. Topside: RM Young anemometers (Marine and Heavy Duty); Campbell Scientific GPS16x-HVS; LI-COR 190R PAR. Surface: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO); SBE ECO FLNTU; SBE SUNA V2 nitrate; Teledyne RDI ADCP 600 kHz; Triaxys directional wave sensor. Bottom: SBE 37-SMP MicroCAT (CTD, DO), 66 ft; SBE HydroCAT-EP (CTD, DO, pH); Sunburst SAMI pCO2.
